title: The Twelve Sent Out
summary: Jesus gives his twelve disciples authority to heal and drive out spirits, names them, and sends them to the lost sheep of Israel to announce that the kingdom of heaven is near. He tells them to travel light, to expect rejection, persecution, and division even within families, and not to fear, because their Father knows every sparrow. Whoever receives them receives him.
story: At the end of chapter 9 Jesus told his disciples to pray for workers for the harvest. Now he makes them the workers. The twelve, whom Matthew names here for the first time as a group, are sent to do what Jesus has been doing: to preach the kingdom, heal the sick, and cast out demons. This is the second of the five great teaching blocks in Matthew. The first (chapters 5 to 7) described life in the kingdom; this one describes carrying its message into a world that will not always want it. The instructions begin with a short mission within Israel and widen, from verse 16 on, into warnings about governors, kings, and Gentiles that reach far past this first trip toward the church's later mission.
historical:
The mission is limited at first to Israel, avoiding the Gentiles and the Samaritans. The Samaritans lived in the hill country between Galilee and Judea; they worshiped the God of Israel but held only the five books of Moses as Scripture and worshiped on Mount Gerizim rather than in Jerusalem, and relations between them and Jews were hostile. The warnings about councils, synagogues, governors, and kings fit the conditions of the first century. Local Jewish councils could discipline members of their communities, including by flogging (Deuteronomy 25:2-3 set a limit of forty lashes, and Paul says in 2 Corinthians 11:24 that he received thirty-nine lashes five times). Roman governors such as Pontius Pilate, prefect of Judea from AD 26 to 36, and client kings such as Herod Antipas and later Herod Agrippa I held power over life and death, and the book of Acts records apostles brought before exactly such authorities.

The list of the twelve also appears in Mark 3:16-19, Luke 6:14-16, and Acts 1:13. The lists agree on most names; where Matthew and Mark have Thaddaeus, Luke and Acts have Judas son of James, and most interpreters think these are the same man known by two names. Simon is called the Zealot, from an Aramaic word meaning zealous. Whether that marks him as a former member of a revolutionary faction or simply as a man zealous for the law is debated, since the Zealot party as an organized movement is clearly attested by the historian Josephus only in the Jewish war with Rome that began in AD 66. The meaning of Iscariot is also uncertain; the most common suggestion is that it means man of Kerioth, a town in southern Judea.
cultural:
Travelers in the ancient world carried money in their belts, a bag for provisions, a spare tunic, sandals, and a staff for walking and defense. Jesus tells the twelve to go without these and to depend on the hospitality of those who receive them, a custom deeply rooted in the Near East. Their peace, spoken as a greeting (shalom), was understood as more than a pleasantry; it was a blessing that could rest on a house or return to the one who gave it. Shaking the dust off one's feet was a symbolic act of separation, a public sign that the town had rejected the message and would answer for it.

The sparrow was among the cheapest food sold in the market. The coin named in verse 29 is the assarion, a small Roman copper coin worth one-sixteenth of a denarius, which was roughly a laborer's daily wage. Hell here translates Gehenna, the Valley of Hinnom just south of Jerusalem, where some kings of Judah had burned children in sacrifice (2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31); by Jesus' day its name had become a picture of final judgment. The cross in verse 38 would have meant only one thing to a first-century hearer: the Roman method of execution for slaves and rebels, in which the condemned man carried the beam to his own death.
literary: The chapter is a speech, framed by narrative at its start and closed in 11:1 with the formula Matthew uses to end each of his five discourses (compare 7:28, 13:53, 19:1, 26:1). It moves in three stages. Verses 5 to 15 give practical instructions for the immediate mission. Verses 16 to 23 widen into persecution before governors and Gentiles. Verses 24 to 42 turn to the disciple's identity: like teacher, like disciple; fear God rather than people; loyalty to Jesus above family; and the promise that even a cup of cold water given to a disciple will be rewarded. The repeated command “do not be afraid” (verses 26, 28, 31) forms a pattern at the center. Much of the material in verses 17 to 42 has parallels scattered in Mark 13 and in Luke 12 and 14, which suggests that Matthew has gathered sayings on mission into one address.

outline.t: The twelve apostles named and given authority
Instructions for the mission to Israel
Do not be afraid: the Father's care and public confession
Not peace but a sword: the cost of following
Receiving the messengers and their reward

doctrines.note: The mission of the church begins as a sharing in Jesus' own mission: the same message, the same authority, the same dependence on God. The limit to Israel is temporary and reflects the order of God's promises; the risen Jesus will send them to all nations in 28:19.

Not one sparrow falls to the ground apart from the Father, and the hairs of the disciples' heads are numbered. God's care extends to the smallest details, which is the ground for courage in persecution rather than a promise that persecution will not come.

The chapter speaks soberly of the day of judgment, of Gehenna, and of Jesus confessing or denying people before his Father. Response to Jesus' messengers is response to Jesus himself, and it carries eternal weight.

words.note: Apostolos, apostle, one who is sent. The word is related to the verb apostello, to send, used in verses 5, 16, and 40. An apostle is an authorized messenger who carries the authority of the sender, which is why receiving them means receiving Jesus. Matthew uses the noun only here.

Geenna, Gehenna, the Greek form of the Hebrew name for the Valley of Hinnom. It is the most common word Jesus uses for final judgment. The point in verse 28 is that God, not human persecutors, has final authority over a person's whole existence.

Stauros, cross. This is the first time the word appears in Matthew, before Jesus has predicted his own death. To take up one's cross meant to accept public shame and death, and Jesus sets that as the shape of following him.

Homologeo, to confess or acknowledge publicly. The word means to say the same thing, to agree openly. In verses 32 and 33 it is paired with arneomai, to deny, and describes a courtroom-like scene in which Jesus acknowledges before the Father those who acknowledged him before others.

christ: The chapter shows Jesus as the one with authority to share his authority. He does not only heal; he empowers others to heal in his name. His messengers carry his presence, so that receiving them is receiving him and, through him, the Father who sent him, a claim no prophet of Israel made for himself. The warnings about being handed over, flogged, and brought before governors describe what will happen to Jesus himself in chapters 26 and 27, and the call to take up the cross anticipates his own. Micah 7:6, quoted in verses 35 and 36, described the breakdown of trust in a corrupt generation; Jesus applies it to the division his coming will cause, as loyalty to him cuts across even the strongest bonds. The saying about losing one's life to find it is the pattern of his death and resurrection, laid over the lives of his followers.

hard.q: What did Jesus mean by “you will not reach all the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes”?
hard.a: Verse 23 is one of the most debated sayings in the Gospels, because it seems to set a short time limit on the coming of the Son of Man. Albert Schweitzer, in his study of the historical Jesus published in 1906, took it as evidence that Jesus expected the end of the world during this mission and was disappointed. Most Christian interpreters have read it differently. Some take the coming as Jesus' vindication in his resurrection and exaltation, since Daniel 7 describes the son of man coming to God to receive a kingdom, and in 28:18 the risen Jesus announces that all authority has been given to him. Others connect it with the judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70, which Jesus links with the Son of Man's coming in chapter 24. Others read it as a statement about the mission to Israel lasting until his return at the end of the age, so that the task will not be finished before he comes. Each view has defenders among careful scholars, and the chapter's own widening scope, reaching beyond the first mission to governors and Gentiles, is part of what makes the verse hard to pin down.

questions: Jesus told the twelve to take almost nothing and rely on others' welcome. What would it look like for you to depend on others in the work God gives you?
Three times Jesus says “do not be afraid.” What fears most shape how openly you speak about your faith?
Jesus warns that loyalty to him can divide families. How do you honor your family while keeping him first?
